newsitem.title: UK: Sterling hovers below 2.81 marks, $1.64 in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Sterling hovers below 2.81 marks, $1.64 in Europe.

text.p: Sterling wobbled, easing below 2.81 marks and $1.64 after a smaller-than-expected drop in British unemployment and steady earnings dampened expectations of higher rates, said analysts.

"With the smaller-than-expected fall in jobless... The market now takes the view that the Bank of England will not hike rates immediately in July," said Claudio Demolli, foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch.
Last week the BoE raised base rates to 6.50 percent from 6.25, and economists have said more hikes are needed to thwart inflation unless the government tightens fiscal policy in its July budget.
At 1130 GMT, sterling/mark was at 2.8075/85 against 2.8168/73 in late Europe on Tuesday, while cable was at $1.6352/62 against $1.6374/84.

UK unemployment fell by 18,400 to 1.64 million in May for an unemployment rate of 5.8 percent, the lowest rate in almost seven years. This, however, compared with expectations for a drop of 40,000. Average earnings growth, moreover, was steady at 4.5 percent in the year to April.
"The average earnings figures were quite weak... On balance they should moderate (rate) expectations," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Investment Bank.

"Inflation is unlikely to get out of hand given the new credibility in monetary policy, while on the fiscal side, a modest tightening of policy in the budget should improve (inflation) sentiment further," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

Traders said much of sterling's fortunes were pinned to the dollar, which skidded to its lowest in nearly seven months to 110.62 yen on concerns about Japan's widening trade surplus with the U.S. The move weighed on sterling/mark and sterling/yen, which sank to fresh six-month troughs of 181.59 in early Europe. Cable, however, got a slight lift from the dollar's woes.
Despite sterling's stumble, analysts said yield differentials would continue to keep the unit buoyant in Europe.

"Certainly against the European currencies, sterling may still make gains. It is benefiting from high interest rates combined with what is seen as a relatively solid economy," said Chase Investment's Schmidt.
